name: Green tea / EGCG

lead: Green tea and its main catechin, EGCG, are taken as a gentle thermogenic for fat loss, either as tea or as concentrated capsule extracts.
Most published work on EGCG is laboratory or animal research, and the sources reviewed contain no completed human trial showing an appearance effect.

paras: EGCG is absorbed in the intestine and metabolised with help from gut bacteria; oral absorption is poor. Cell and mouse studies report anti-inflammatory and metabolic effects, which have not been established in people for appearance.

EFSA stated in 2018 that 800 mg or more of EGCG daily could increase liver-damage risk, and green tea catechins are among the ingredients most implicated in supplement-related liver injury. The FDA has sent warning letters to EGCG makers over disease claims.

lead: Epigallocatechin gallate (EGCG) is the most abundant catechin in tea, a polyphenol formed from epigallocatechin and gallic acid. Dried green tea leaves contain about 7,380 mg per 100 g, far more than black tea, in which most catechins are converted during processing.[1] Green tea and concentrated green tea extracts are sold as mild 'thermogenic' or fat-loss supplements.

Much of the published research on EGCG is laboratory and animal work, for example in diet-induced obese mice.[2] Reviews describe poor oral absorption.[1] Regulators have raised safety concerns about concentrated extracts: the European Food Safety Authority stated in 2018 that daily intakes of 800 mg or more of EGCG could increase the risk of liver damage, and Wikipedia's supplement overview lists green tea catechins among the ingredients most implicated in supplement-related liver injury.[1][3]
infobox: Sold as a dietary supplement; FDA warning letters issued over disease claims

paras: In looksmaxxing and fitness contexts, green tea extract is promoted as a mild thermogenic for fat loss. It has also been studied for conditions including acne, obesity with high LDL, diabetes, and cancer prevention, listed under Clinical studies below.[4]

EGCG is mainly absorbed in the intestine, and gut bacteria play a role in its metabolism before absorption.[2] Oral bioavailability is poor even at intakes equivalent to 8 to 16 cups of green tea daily, which can cause nausea or heartburn. Blood levels peak after about 1.7 hours, and methylated metabolites can reach 8 to 25 times the plasma level of unmetabolised EGCG.[1]

Laboratory studies report a range of effects, including anti-inflammatory activity and effects on cancer cell lines such as melanoma.[5][6] These are cell and animal findings and are not demonstrations of effects in people.

A 2011 European Food Safety Authority analysis found no demonstrated cause-and-effect link between tea catechins and maintaining normal LDL cholesterol; a 2016 systematic review by Momose and colleagues found small LDL reductions at high doses over 4 to 14 weeks.[1] The sources reviewed contain no meta-analysis of green tea for appearance outcomes.

A 2018 review by Hu and colleagues found that excessive EGCG intake may cause liver toxicity, and considered 338 mg per day safe as a capsule or tablet and 704 mg per day safe as a tea beverage. EFSA estimates a cup of green tea contains about 165 mg of EGCG.[1] Liver injury from weight-loss and bodybuilding supplements most often involves hepatocellular injury, with green tea catechins among the most implicated ingredients.[3]

From 2008 to 2017 the US FDA issued warning letters to EGCG supplement makers, mostly because promotional claims treated or prevented diseases, making the products unapproved new drugs under US law.[1]

Registered human trials of green tea extract or EGCG include a trial in women with acne (NCT01846338, n=80, status unknown),[7] a phase 3 trial in obese women with high LDL (NCT02116517, n=73),[8] a phase 3 trial in type 2 diabetes with hyperlipidemia (NCT01360567, n=102),[9] and trials in colorectal cancer chemoprevention, endometriosis, uterine fibroids, endothelial function, diabetic nephropathy, hepatitis C and asthma.[10][11] The registry entries in the sources reviewed do not report results, so they are not evidence of effect.
Animal work includes a study in which EGCG reduced body weight in diet-induced obese mice,[12] which is not a human trial.

timeline.event: FDA begins issuing warning letters to EGCG supplement makers, continuing to 2017.[1]
EFSA states that daily EGCG intake of 800 mg or more could increase risk of liver damage.[1]
